title: The Jataka, closed
hookLine: the long road of many lives that the Jataka traces to one awakening

lines: AN ELEPHANT, A WOODPECKER, A TREASURER.
A SAGE, A KING, A PRINCE.
cards: An elephant who carries a lost man out of the forest. A woodpecker who pulls a bone from a lion's throat. A treasurer who points at a dead mouse in the street.
A caravan leader in the desert. A clever sage at court. A king who gives away his eyes.
A prince who gives away everything. In the Jataka, they are all the same one: the bodhisatta, the being on the way to becoming the Buddha.

teach.h: AND THE WISE ONE WAS I.
teach.b: Start with how each tale ends. In the Jataka, the Buddha tells a story of the past because of something happening in the present: a monk who's discouraged, a quarrel, a kindness.
When the story is done, he names who everyone was. That monk was the frightened deer. That troublemaker was the jackal.
And the wise one, he says, was I. That last line turns a fable into a birth story. Under the tales runs a road.
Early in these weeks came Sumedha, lying in the mud before an earlier Buddha, setting out on the long way and taking on the perfections he would need.
Every tale since has been one step on that road: generosity here, patience there, truthfulness, effort, wisdom. And the bodhisatta isn't always a king or a sage.

He's an elephant, a bird, a merchant, a minister. The tales let the one on the way to awakening be an animal or an ordinary worker. The collection closes with Vessantara and the gift that cost him nearly everything.
Tradition tells the life after it as the one in which he becomes the Buddha. So the Jataka doesn't end with an awakening.
It ends right before one, with a family coming home from the mountain. Some Buddhists read these stories as history, some as teaching tales, some as both.
Read either way, the collection tells awakening as a long walk, made of small turns in ordinary lives.

how: Buddhist teachers use Jataka tales in sermons, schools and festivals, often telling a tale and then explaining which perfection it shows.

o: a collection of rules for monks
a book of the Buddha's final sermons
the birth stories of the Buddha's past lives

games.q: the Jataka, closed: tap the pairs.
p: why the Buddha tells the tale
set out on the road, lying in the mud
the tale the collection closes with

s: in the Jataka, the bodhisatta is always human
he is an elephant, a woodpecker and other animals too, as well as merchants, ministers and kings.
each tale ends by naming who the characters were
the Buddha links the people of the past to people in the present, and names himself last.
the tales were told only to children
in the Jataka itself, the Buddha tells them to monks and followers about something happening right then.

games.q: the Buddha has just finished telling a tale of the past to his monks. what does he say last?
o: who each character was, and that the wise one was him.
games.why: he names who everyone was, then and now, and ends with himself. that closing link is what makes a fable a birth story.

practice: Let the stories of these weeks pass by: the dead mouse, the monkey gardeners, the donkey in the lion's skin, the sky that was falling, the six-tusked elephant, Maddi in the forest.
Don't choose the one you think you should; notice which one comes back, and say to yourself, in one sentence, why.

wordCard.voice: The Jataka. The birth stories: one being across many lives, every tale a step on the road to awakening. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: a being bound for awakening, the hero of every Jataka. Sanskrit: bodhisattva.

carryVoice: Your line: many lives, one road. Every tale was a step along it. See you tomorrow.
